This week, your AI agent will probably do something you did not approve.

Persistent agents just landed in the CRM. Salesforce shipped agents that read sales records and follow up on their own. OpenAI rolled out persistent dots. GitLab 19.4 hits October 19 with governance controls that meter every workflow your agent runs.

The pilot era is over. Your agent is now doing work.

The question for Q4 is no longer "should we deploy agents?" It is "what guardrails ship before they do?"

Here is what we are watching this week, and what we are advising clients to lock in before October ends:

1. Governance before scale. GitLab's move is the preview. Every agent needs a kill switch, an audit trail, and a budget. If yours does not, that is sprint one.

2. Narrow the scope. The 95% GenAI pilot failure rate is not because the tech failed. It is because teams tried to automate everything. Pick one workflow. Earn the second.

3. Keep humans in the loop on contracts, payments, and hiring. Everything else becomes a clean handoff.

The companies pulling ahead this quarter are not the ones running the most agents. They are the ones running the cleanest rules.

What is one workflow you are letting your agent run unsupervised this week? Drop it in the comments, and we will send back three guardrails you can deploy in 48 hours.

LinkedIn's CEO said something that stopped me:

"Every job is going to be a new job."

He's right. The skills employers are hiring for are changing faster than the skills on candidates' profiles. As he put it: "Your needs and the roles you're hiring for are evolving at twice the rate of the labor you're trying to tap into."

That's a supply and demand mismatch of historic proportions.

But here's what most people are missing:

The professionals winning in this market aren't the ones with the most AI skills. They're the ones who can translate their existing expertise into the new language of AI-augmented work.

A Sales professional who understands AI tools isn't replaced by AI. They become the person who knows how to sell AI solutions.

An HR leader who can navigate AI-assisted hiring isn't obsolete. They become the person who builds the human-AI collaboration framework.

A Finance analyst who can interpret AI-generated insights isn't redundant. They become the person who turns data into strategic decisions.

The question isn't whether your job will change. It's whether you'll be the one to shape how it changes.

The most misunderstood force reshaping AI in 2026 is not the model itself. It is the shift from "copilots" that assist to autonomous agents that execute, and the structural tension this creates inside every organization.

I have been working hands-on with teams deploying these agents for real-time operations. The non-obvious lesson is that autonomy is not a technical switch you flip. It is a trust model you earn. When an agent can negotiate a supplier contract, re-route a shipment, or adjust a pricing tier without human review, the organization must be redesigned around a fundamentally different risk profile. The teams that succeed are not the ones with the best model accuracy. They are the ones that have built a "delegation framework" that defines exactly what decisions an agent can own, under what conditions, and with what fallback.

The latest releases, including faster inference models and agents that can reason across video, audio, and text in real time, make this transition inevitable. But the bottleneck is no longer capability. It is the organizational muscle to trust an agent with a decision that previously required a senior manager. I have seen teams run "digital rehearsals" where a simulated agent interacts with a historical dataset of past decisions, and the output reveals that the agent would have made a better call 60% of the time. Yet the team still hesitates to deploy.

Another trend reshaping the field is the emergence of "vibe coding" as a legitimate production practice. Engineers are no longer writing every line of code. They are describing intent, letting the model generate the implementation, and then validating the output. This changes the skill profile of a senior engineer from "writes the most complex code" to "defines the most precise constraints." The candidates who will win in this market are the ones who can specify a problem boundary, not just fill a function.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the person who can prompt a model or deploy a container. You need someone who has designed a delegation framework for autonomous agents, who understands how to simulate and validate agent behavior before production, and who can build the organizational systems that allow autonomy to scale without chaos. I am actively exploring the next challenge where I can apply these agent-systems principles to help a team move from copilot experiments to autonomous operations.

Where Should We Not Use AI?

Everyone is discussing where AI should be used; in my opinion, we should also consider where it shouldn't be.
Although AI is powerful, that doesn't mean it is always an advantage to use it in every case. In certain situations, handing the task over to AI can eliminate the human judgment, responsibility, empathy, or experience that makes the task valuable in the first place.
Here are some places where I would be very careful, or avoid using AI altogether:
1. Helping you to make major life decisions. While AI can help you consider your options, it shouldn't decide whether you should marry someone, end a relationship, move to another country, quit your job, or make any other deeply personal decision.
2. AI can help you organize your thoughts when you need to apologize, give feedback, settle a conflict, or let someone know how you feel; however, you still have to carry out the conversation.
3. You can't judge a person's character based on limited information. If you give an AI several messages and then ask it, "Is this person toxic?" or "Is my partner a narcissist?", you will end up with a false sense of certainty about complicated human behavior.
4. It is not advisable to make medical decisions without the involvement of a qualified professional. While AI can help explain medical terms or prepare questions for your doctor, diagnosis, treatment changes, medicayou should not leave ation decisions, or emergency care to a chatbot.
5. Making legal decisions without proper scrutiny is one thing; using AI to understand a contract is something else, but relying on it alone for a lawsuit, an immigration matter, a tax problem, or a legally binding agreement is quite different.
6. People should not be assessed in high-stakes situations without human supervision. Matters such as hiring, firing, promotion, lending, insurance, education, and other decisions that have a major impact on someone's life must not be left to AI's judgment as a black-box system.
7. Every personal message is written. If AI produces all the birthday messages, condolence notes, thank-you notes, messages of love, and apologies, communication might become efficient but emotionally empty.
8. Replacing learning with answer generation: asking the AI for the final answer each time may make you faster now but will make you weaker later on. Sometimes, real learning comes from struggling with the problem.
I am highly optimistic about AI, but I don't believe the aim should be to apply it in every aspect of life.
Perhaps we should ask: "Does AI enhance this task, or does it take away something important from it?"
The wisest application of AI is knowing when it's appropriate not to use it.

Not everything should be automated.

A useful rule:

Automate actions. Keep judgment human.

Good automation:

→ Move information
→ Create records
→ Generate drafts
→ Route requests
→ Send notifications
→ Update systems
→ Calculate values
→ Schedule follow-ups

Be more careful automating:

→ Hiring decisions
→ Large purchases
→ Sensitive customer responses
→ Contract approval
→ Financial exceptions
→ Anything where context matters more than speed

A great workflow often looks like this:

System gathers information
→ AI summarizes it
→ Human reviews it
→ Human approves
→ Automation handles everything afterward

The goal isn't removing humans.

It's putting humans where they're most valuable.

Two companies just agreed to spend at least $2 billion so one can sit inside the other and watch the machine get built.
That is either prudence or the most expensive hall monitor in modern corporate history.

Anthropic says its partnership with Accenture is non-exclusive, announced Friday, and it is the first independent evaluation arrangement for Anthropic’s frontier AI. Each side is putting up at least $1 billion over the next five years for what Dario Amodei calls “embedded evaluation.” Employee-like access. Safety verification. Incident reporting. Public accounting of benefits and risks. Clean language, huge check, and enough vagueness to make a board deck blush.

Anthropic says Accenture will have access comparable to an employee’s, can follow decisions on how models are built and deployed, and can report incidents. Anthropic also says it will fund Accenture directly, while talking with METR and other nonprofit evaluators using their own funding. OpenAI has committed to the same concept, and Sam Altman called it a “great idea.”

Picture a founder telling the audit committee, “Trust us,” then hiring someone to sit in the conference room with a badge, a laptop, and permission to open the wrong door. Suddenly trust gets a spreadsheet.

I get the temptation. Every ambitious man wants maximum speed with just enough oversight to keep the lenders calm and the critics off the org chart. I do too.

But this is what serious power looks like. When companies say the evaluator is independent while the company funds the work directly, pay attention to the noun and the verb. Independence under contract has a funny walk.

Still, the ordinary employee inside these organizations deserves honest guardrails. So does the man whose retirement account, tax bill, or freedom will eventually feel the downstream effects of whatever gets signed off in those rooms.

If you build, govern it. If you fund, verify it. And if you hear “employee-like access,” picture a badge opening the door your son may one day have to walk through.

Every engineering manager’s inbox is about to get flooded with this headline.
A new macroeconomic study released yesterday, covered by InfoWorld, estimates that AI will boost software engineer productivity by 32.6%.

It won't take long for leadership and finance teams to ask: "If our engineers are 32.6% more productive, why isn't our roadmap shipping 32.6% faster? Can we freeze hiring?"
Over 20 years in software engineering, I’ve seen this exact cycle play out with Agile, offshore delivery models, and Cloud migrations: the industry confuses task acceleration with end-to-end delivery velocity.

Here is what the macroeconomic models miss about how software gets built in the real world:
1. Amdahl’s Law Still Governs Software Delivery
Writing code is only 20% to 30% of a software engineer's actual job. The other 70% is alignment: clarifying vague product requirements, negotiating cross-team API contracts, threat modeling, conducting code reviews, debugging distributed race conditions, and monitoring deployments. Even if AI made the typing portion 10x faster, the unaccelerated 70% still dictates overall time-to-market.
2. The Jevons Paradox: Cheaper Code Creates More Demand, Not Less Work
In economics, when technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, total consumption of that resource rises rather than falls. Making code cheaper to produce doesn't mean we need fewer engineers; it means the business suddenly demands more experiments, deeper integrations, more personalization, and higher reliability.
3. The Downstream Quality Tax
If a team rushes to capture that 32% speedup without strengthening automated verification, they end up creating a flood of pull requests that bottleneck code reviews, overload QA, and increase rollback frequencies.

As technical leaders, how do we steer this conversation constructively with executive leadership?

Here are three ways we can frame the "AI Productivity Dividend":
* Measure Value Delivered, Not PR Velocity: Shift the leadership conversation away from "lines of code" or "tickets closed per sprint" to business outcomes: customer retention, latency reduction, and revenue-enabling platform capabilities.
* Reinvest the Dividend in System Health: Use the time saved on boilerplate to pay down accumulated tech debt, fortify automated test harnesses, and eliminate brittle legacy dependencies that cause 2 AM pages.
* Educate Stakeholders on Cognitive Bandwidth: Explain that AI removes mechanical friction, but high-impact architecture, domain modeling, and user empathy still require human judgment, focus, and time.

How is your leadership team viewing AI productivity metrics? Are your stakeholders expecting immediate headcount savings or higher roadmap velocity—and how are you bridging the gap?

Today I complete 4 years building and architecting software for businesses across multiple industries. 🎉

It wasn't smooth. It started with a bad decision.
NDA. JEE. Agriculture entrances. I prepared for all three at once and cleared none. Terrible strategy. But it showed me my potential, my worth, and my discipline.

Then came the reality check.
In college, I didn't know the first thing about code. Classmates had been coding since school and wrote programs in one go. I was struggling with concepts while they built full-stack projects.
Then lockdown hit, and I locked myself in too. Explored Languages, databases, networking, development, architecture, and many more, all while attending online classes. 📚

After few months, followed the standard strategy to get an Internship. 
So I chased internships. I got exactly one, in Android development, against many attempts. 😅 It showed me how real industry works from the inside.

Placement season: everyone went left, I went right.
Everyone was targeting stable organizations. I picked something unique and niche: a Blockchain Startup. 
There I worked on every layer: development, architecture, management, and discussions with stakeholders. I built protocols, private chains, contracts, SDKs, etc... for supply chain, financing, agreements, real-world asset bindings, tokenomics, and many more. ⛓️

Next goal: become a Full Stack Web3 Engineer.
New organization, same hunger, bigger scope. I led teams across projects, kept building, architecting, and additionally involved in hiring processes.

Then I saw where the world was heading: AI and Quantum. ⚛️
I joined a Quantum-focused organization with zero cybersecurity knowledge, but Web3 had already given me strong cryptography. That was my bridge.
People usually take weeks or months to understand the stack, product, and use-cases. I started contributing within 3-4 days. A few weeks later, I was in the core team, which is responsible for decoding use-cases, architecture and directions, working on RFPs and demos, client calls, leading teams, hiring, and streamlining the entire lifecycle across teams.

Notice the pattern?
Every "I'm behind" moment pushed me into the next move. 🔁
These years changed my personality. I solve real problems, talk to people with confidence, and take initiative instead of waiting to be told. 

My simple philosophy:
1️⃣ Work like you're building your own product, don't look at clock for tracking typical 9 hours.
2️⃣ If someone pays you ₹100, deliver ₹150. The right people will recognize the efforts. And, prove their risky bet on you was right.
3️⃣ Keep contributing until you are satisfied.
4️⃣ Never stop learning.

Many more years ahead with the same mindset. Cheers! 🥂

Regulated AI has more than one customer. The employee wants an answer, IT wants control, compliance wants the trail, and the examiner wants to know how the answer happened.

Go.AI has raised an $85M Series A led by Updata Partners for that crowded buying committee. Existing investors GFT Ventures and LAUNCH returned, bringing the company's disclosed funding to $90M. Updata General Partner Carter Griffin will join the board.

David Moscatelli and Lisa Gillespie built the company around a blunt constraint: banks, credit unions, healthcare systems and other regulated organizations cannot treat every AI workload like a casual trip through someone else's cloud.

Go.AI combines the Go1 appliance with Go.OS, an operating system for models, indexing, applications and audit records inside the customer's environment. The company sells fixed infrastructure rather than a per-token meter, with local and air-gapped configurations.

The product pitch sounds simple because the operating problem is not. Security needs the data path, model-risk teams need governance, compliance needs records, and IT needs infrastructure it can maintain. The buyer needs all of them to keep saying yes after procurement gets serious.

Go.AI says more than 200 customers process over 12.5M queries a day on its infrastructure. It reports ARR growth above 8x year over year, continued profitability and 900,000 monthly users. Updata repeated the ARR, profitability and query figures.

Those are company and investor claims, not audited financial results. Go.AI has not disclosed revenue, the prior-year ARR base, retention, customer concentration, margins, contract values, deployment count or valuation. Activity is visible; the unit economics are not.

The capital will expand engineering, accelerate the Go.OS and Go1 roadmap, grow go-to-market capacity and push beyond regulated industries into a broader set of compliance-minded organizations. Current hiring spans client advisory, field deployment, sales engineering, marketing and strategy.

That hiring mix matters. Hardware has to arrive, networks have to cooperate, policies have to survive real workflows, updates need control, and somebody has to produce the receipts when an examiner asks.

Go.AI is putting $85M behind a market thesis that enterprise AI will split on accountability as much as capability. The next layer belongs to companies that can tell a customer where the model ran, what it touched, how the cost behaves and who owns the answer inside a regulated decision.

AI is making software cheaper to build — and changing where the real value sits
AI coding tools and agents have sharply reduced the cost and time of implementation. Boilerplate, tests, refactors, and first-pass features can now be generated in a fraction of the previous effort. Many developers already report that AI writes a large share of their code. Experimentation is cheaper, internal builds are more viable, and the barrier to turning an idea into working software has dropped.
The bottleneck has simply moved. Writing code is faster. Reviewing, validating, securing, and integrating that code is not. The scarce skills are shifting toward precise specification, system design, critical review of AI output, and long-term maintainability. Engineers who mainly produce code face declining leverage. Those who can define problems clearly, evaluate generated work, and own architectural judgment gain it.
This shift also changes the employment equation.
In a traditional permanent role, a large part of the value an engineer delivered was steady code production inside a fixed process. As that production becomes heavily automated, the remaining high-value work — architecture, review, product judgment, complex problem-solving — becomes more portable and project-based. Companies will need less continuous headcount for routine implementation and more targeted expertise for specific outcomes.
Freelance and contract work fits this new shape better in many cases:
You can specialize in high-leverage skills rather than generalist maintenance.
Clients pay for defined results instead of time spent in meetings and process overhead.
You can work across multiple problems and stacks instead of being locked into one codebase and one company’s constraints.
As AI lowers the cost of building, more companies (especially smaller ones and startups) will prefer flexible external talent over full-time hiring for many initiatives.
Permanent roles will still exist, particularly for core platform ownership and deep domain knowledge. But the relative advantage of long-term employment weakens when implementation capacity is abundant and the highest-value contributions are episodic and skill-specific.
Software is becoming cheaper to produce. The higher-value work is moving toward judgment, design, and verification — work that travels well outside a single company’s walls.
The engineers who adapt will treat AI as leverage, not replacement, and structure their careers around portable expertise rather than permanent seat time.
